newsitem.title: UK: British Conservatives open key pre-poll conference.
newsitem.headline: British Conservatives open key pre-poll conference.

text.p: Britain's ruling Conservatives began a crucial pre-election conference on Tuesday lagging in opinion polls, at loggerheads over Europe and demoralised by allegations of political sleaze.
Party chairman Brian Mawhinney tried to boost confidence by declaring: "This is a party that is on its way to winning the next election."
But as delegates filed into the conference centre in the resort of Bournemouth, the newspapers they carried were filled with gloom for the party.

And the conference was overshadowed by Monday's suspected Irish Republican car bomb attacks on Northern Ireland's army headquarters in which 31 people were injured, threatening the already fragile peace process in which Prime Minister John Major had invested so much political capital.
The Guardian newspaper carried a poll that put the Conservatives 18 points behind the opposition Labour Party with at most eight months go go to a general election.
In the Times, John Redwood, the right-winger who last year challenged Major for the party leadership, criticised Major's wait-and-see policy towards a planned Single European Currency.
"If in a meeting there is a heated argument going on, you will not be heard if you occasionally murmur that you have not yet made up your mind," he said.

The article confirmed the gap between Redwood and Major, apparent on Monday when Redwood seemed to hesitate in a television interview about advising electors to back the Conservatives at the election.
"I think you will have to ask me that nearer the time," he said before adding when pressed: "Of course I will answer. Vote for the Conservative Party."

In all papers there was speculation that a "Eurosceptic" Conservative MP, James Cran, had stepped down as an aide to Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Patrick Mayhew because of disagreement with aspects of government policy.

Mawhinney, speaking on BBC television, said the government would not yield to pressure from Redwood and others to rule out British membership of the new single currency at least for the next parliament.
"Government policy has been set out by the cabinet, by the Prime Minister, by a number of us time and time again. It is not going to change," he said.
"It is not going to change because it is in the best national interest that we should make the decision on the single currency when all the information is available."
Mawhinney also said he had spoken to Cran, who is abroad. "He wanted me to say on his behalf that he supports the government and there is no disagreement on policy," he said.
Cran had left Mayhew because he needed to spend time getting to know the new constituency he will fight at the next election, Mawhinney said.
